concept_card.subtopic: Restoring force and the defining condition a = −ω²x
concept_card.learning_objective: Students will be able to state that the restoring force in SHM is proportional to displacement and always directed toward the mean position, and use a = −ω²x with ω² = k/m to find acceleration at any displacement.
concept_card.statement: In SHM the restoring force F = −kx grows with displacement and always points toward the mean position, so a = −ω²x with ω² = k/m.
concept_card.simple: Pull a block on a spring and let go. The spring always pulls it back toward the middle. The farther you pull, the harder it pulls back. At the middle, the pull is zero.
concept_card.formal: A particle performs SHM when the net force on it is a restoring force proportional to its displacement from the mean position and opposite in direction: F = −kx. By Newton's second law, ma = −kx, so a = −(k/m)x = −ω²x, where ω = √(k/m) is the angular frequency. The condition a ∝ −x defines SHM. The acceleration is zero at the mean and has maximum magnitude ω²A at the extremes, whatever the direction of velocity.

equations.meaning: Restoring force is proportional to displacement and opposite to it
Defining condition of SHM: acceleration proportional to displacement, directed toward the mean
Angular frequency is fixed by the stiffness and the mass

concept_card.analogy: A ball in a round bowl: wherever you push it, the slope always tips it back toward the bottom, and the farther up the side, the steeper the slope and the stronger the tip back.
steps: Locate the mean position and measure the displacement x from it
The restoring force is F = −kx: its size is k|x| and its direction is toward the mean
Ignore which way the body is moving; only the displacement sets the force
Check: zero at the mean, largest (ω²A) at the extremes
concept_card.worked_example: m = 0.25 kg, k = 100 N/m, block at x = +0.03 m. F = −kx = −100 × 0.03 = −3 N (toward mean). ω² = k/m = 400 s⁻², so ω = 20 rad/s and a = −ω²x = −400 × 0.03 = −12 m/s², i.e. 12 m/s² toward the mean.
alternatives: Think of the spring as always trying to undo the stretch: it pulls in when stretched and pushes out when compressed, so the force always points back to the natural length, and a bigger stretch means a bigger correction.
On an a–x graph, SHM is a straight line through the origin with negative slope −ω²; any other shape (constant a, positive slope, curve) is not SHM.

remediation_cards.wrong_idea: The spring pulls back with the same force everywhere, because k doesn't change.
remediation_cards.why_it_feels_right: k is a constant, so a constant pull seems natural.
remediation_cards.why_wrong: The force is k times the displacement: double the stretch, double the force; zero at the mean.
remediation_cards.correct_idea: The restoring force F = −kx is proportional to displacement: zero at the mean and largest at the extremes.
remediation_cards.sim_moment: Watch the acceleration arrow shrink to nothing at the mean and grow longest at the extremes.

remediation_cards.wrong_idea: The force acts the way the block is moving, so when it moves outward the force is outward too.
remediation_cards.why_it_feels_right: We push things the way we want them to move, so force and motion seem to go together.
remediation_cards.why_wrong: Force sets acceleration, not velocity. Moving outward, the block slows down, so the force points back to the mean.
remediation_cards.correct_idea: The restoring force always points toward the mean, whichever way the block moves.
remediation_cards.sim_moment: Pause while the block moves outward: it heads out, but the acceleration arrow points back to the mean.

contrast_probes.probe: As the block moves from the mean out to the extreme, what happens to the restoring force?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: Nothing changes, it's the same force all the way out.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: It keeps pushing the block outward, that's why it reaches the extreme.

contrast_probes.probe: How does the restoring force at 1 cm from the mean compare with the force at 4 cm?
contrast_probes.reply_if_first: They're equal, the spring is the same so the force is the same.
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: At 4 cm it's four times bigger, since F is proportional to x.

contrast_probes.probe: While the block is moving outward, past the mean toward the extreme, which way does the force on it point?
contrast_probes.reply_if_second: Back toward the mean, which is why the block slows down and stops at the extreme.

doubts.q: If the force always pulls toward the mean, why doesn't the block just stop at the mean?
doubts.a: At the mean the force is zero but the speed is maximum. By inertia the block overshoots, and only then does the restoring force start slowing it down on the other side.

doubts.q: What does the minus sign in F = −kx actually mean?
doubts.a: It means the force is opposite to the displacement. If x is positive the force is negative, and vice versa, so the force always points back to the mean.

doubts.q: At the extreme the velocity is zero, so isn't the acceleration also zero there?
doubts.a: No. Acceleration depends on displacement, not velocity. At the extreme x = ±A, so the acceleration has its largest magnitude, ω²A, directed toward the mean.

No. It is SHM only if the acceleration is proportional to displacement and opposite to it, a = −ω²x. A ball bouncing on the floor is periodic but not SHM, because its acceleration is g, which does not depend on x.
